Sounds like a bitter first attempt to making a "fun" deck thinking that
as you're playing with a "fun" deck, nobody should beat you because of
that, and because you didn't bother with pool/blood gain and no bleed
nor combat defense, not to mention anything that would actually oust
your prey ;)

: Meanwhile, as I said in the other post, the best multiplayer TCG is

: Shadowfist. Everyone gets to play the game until it's complete and
: the process is usually more upbeat - building to a crescendo rather
: than fading into nothingness.

Most games work a bit like Chez Geek (for example). Everyone goes
forward and the first to cross the line wins. In most games there's
either little you can do to stop someone from winning with interesting
mechanics or table dynamics or, the outcome of the game is determined
mostly by luck and the cards people (happen to) have in hand. Games like
these wont last very long as anything but casual entertainment in a bar
twice a year.

A good Jyhad game is nothing like that. Instead of one "building to a
crescendo" arc (as you describe it), a Jyhad game has a multitude and
every change in the game affects the game state. True, palyers drop from
the game before the game is finished, but with an experienced table
no-one should get out without a good fight. If you get a crappy start
it's built into the table dynamics that other players have an interest
for keeping you going and alive until you're back on your feet. If they
shrug and let you die, they aren't either thinking straight when they
play or they weren't thinking straight when they build a deck without
options to influence the game - or, as mentioned earlier, you built a
squishy deck and can only blame yourself =)

You misunderstand me - I don't mind games which take over an hour - I
was quite happy playing a four hour Shadowfist game the other weekend.
But it wouldn't have been so much fun if it had been Vampire and one
or more players had to sit out for most of that time.

Your estimates of Vampire game length seem understated. There's a
current thread observing that many tournament games are timing out
with the current time limit of two hours. And, in the finals, where
we may suppose all the players to be experienced, even more time is
required, it seems. But it's not the length of time that's the
problem so much as the fact that players are eliminated during this
time and so can't play any more.

>I _do_ like LA Williams' "Hopping Vampire", though, even if it does
>have two legs...

That art was wrong. Chinese Hopping Vampires are so-called because
they have rigor mortis, not because they have one leg. There's a more
accurate picture on the remake of this card in the latest expansion.
But it's Doomtown which did this best with its Gyonshee card -
excellent art by Dan Frazier (the guy who did Magic's Jester's Cap,
Jyhad's Change of Target and Shadowfist's Neutron Bomb).

>Conversely, dog-piling a single player is much easier (even encouraged) in
>Shadowfist's environment.

You can dog-pile in Shadowfist but it's not especially rewarding as
there are no points for ousting someone in that game and it's almost
impossible to do. Players can bounce back quite quickly and I get
lots of practise at that myself, as I'm often a tall poppy. If you're
worried about this then it's easy to pack your deck with cards that
let you thrive upon punishment - like a bloodstained HK movie hero or
Hollywood terminator type. Hence card titles like "Is that All You
Got?" and "That Which Does Not Kill Me..."

Andrew

#5 - Lord of the Rings

I'm sure it can be played multiplayer. Have never seen it myself.

#4 - Magic

*shrug* Not a multiplayer CCG by nature but played so many different ways I
can give it a pass for being in the top 5.

#3 - A Game of Thrones

I think people have figured out a way to make multiplayer *not* suck by messing
with the rules some. I don't know if they ever became official or not.

I can see this making the list. For one thing, there aren't really that many
notable multiplayer CCGs. It's actually a more competitive market than
two-players because you need more opponents, so you get more established
groups, and you get less frenzy for cards (less profit). But, is it better
than 'fist? I have a hard time with that, though maybe being too close to the
game creates a bias.

Mythos - fairly whack in certain ways and very possibly quite broken, still the

its rep or its presentation, much rather play HeroQuest (the boardgame) if I'm

expend to amass offensive and defensive resources in VTES is also what keeps
you in the game. If we are assuming well-matched, good players, we can also

No. The rules indicate that Vampire can be played by two players and

No. All players will tend to upset the equibrium of a game, since equilibrium
isn't a natural state of Fist (it requires a lot of work to maintain, and it's
often better strategy to improve your positon at the cost of pushing the game
out of equilibirum...or to push the game out of equilibrium in hopes of being
able to steal a march on the players who will be damaged by this.

They can do other things, though. They can launch votes that end up hurting
some players drastically more than others; can become another player's puppet
and end up tilting the game in their direction without ever having a chance
of actually winning; can burn vampires on all sides of them creating a power
vacuum that other players exploit simply by virtue of position, can manage,
with a few lucky bleeds, to eliminate a player who might otherwise have been a
contender before being removed from the situation...

VTES to a player who accomplishes a great deal, but with no understanding in
Shadowfist.

The two are not comparable -- a Fist player whose deck is built so badly that
they cannot do anything at all will have no effect on the game at all -- they
will never play their first Feng Shui site, never generate more than the one
point of power they started with, probably never be attacked, and the game
will play pretty much as it would were they not even involved. (by contrast,
a VTES player whose deck is built that badly will at least get to bring out
some vampires, but past that point, is much more likely to stall).

By contrast, a player whose deck works, but is not built with a full
understanding of the game is more likely to produce a game of some type as we
discussed earlier...and a VTES player of similiar level seems pretty likely to
make one of the above errors (after all, isn't stealth/bleed the first deck
almost -everyone- builds?)...or wierder ones, like playing an all malk, all

the throughput ranges are very different, and Fist allows you discard your
entire hand at a moderate cost). I do not consider this a flaw, and this
should not be taken to mean that Shadowfist is "random fun."

Ok, I'll say it flat out: The rate of card play in Fist approaches that of
VTES, and often surpasses it.

Obviously, VTES at the top end can have over a dozen cards get played in a
turn (especially in a combat-heavy deck), but at that rate, you're going to
see deck-exhaustion very fast. And, of course, even a combat-heavy deck will
only get to play all that many cards if it can actually get into a serious
combat (wheras most non-combat-based decks are going to try to use cards like
Majesty to try to stay out of it). Plus, the number of cards you can play
(aside from, and to an extent, even including) is a function of your minions
in play, which only gradually increases over time (even if you're playing a
wenie deck, you'll have to slow down after the first four li'll guys pop out,
though I suppose there may be decks that try to use a combination of
action-based minions and catiffs for explosive growth).

OTOH, In Fist, sure, you only replenish your hand at the beginning of your
turn...but there are plenty of ways of playing cards out of your smoked pile
(where dead and played stuff goes, as distinct from the toasted == out of the
game pile where discarded cards go), events often cost nothing, hand size
increasers are plentiful, and so are ways to bring cards back into your hand.
(and there are also several cards that replenish your hand in mid turn)

So yes, there are also plenty of Fist decks that play a dozen or more
cards per turn at peak output, and more that simply make a dozen or more
actions or spend a few turns playing only a few cards, and then drop 10+ in a
single turn.

VTES, to change the map of the game -- burning vampires, as you mentioned, is
